Calculate $y$ rounded to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's label all of the vertices and sides of our triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/5f7338337e4c6beb9f9fdec8ad952e940162c85058150101c1d083bc83a081f5.png)

The Law of Sines states that

$$
\frac{x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡X}=\frac{y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡Y}=\frac{z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡Z}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
m∠X={78}^{∘},\,m∠Y={36}^{∘},\,x=16,
$$

and consequently

$$
\frac{16}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{78}^{∘}}=\frac{y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}}.
$$

To solve for $y,$ we multiply both sides by $\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}\times \frac{16}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{78}^{∘}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}\times \frac{y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}\times \frac{16}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{78}^{∘}} & =\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}}\times \frac{y}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}}} \\ y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}\times \frac{16}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{78}^{∘}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}≈0.587\,79$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡{78}^{∘}≈0.978\,15,$ both rounded to five decimal places to avoid rounding error. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}\times \frac{16}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{78}^{∘}} \\  & ≈0.587\,79\times \frac{16}{0.978\,15} \\  & ≈\frac{0.587\,79\times 16}{0.978\,15} \\  & ≈\frac{9.404\,64}{0.978\,15} \\  & ≈9.61,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

If the measure of the angle at the point $B$ is ${47}^{∘}$ and the measure of the angle at the point $C$ is ${62}^{∘},$ how far is point $A$ from point $C?$ Round the answer to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/e9674b5a0921c9fb8d936c435351d0557e90984e4662e9a510a6889812bbad38.png)

The Law of Sines states that

$$
\frac{a}{\operatorname{sin}⁡A}=\frac{b}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}=\frac{c}{\operatorname{sin}⁡C}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
m∠B={47}^{∘},\,m∠C={62}^{∘},\,c=20,
$$

and consequently

$$
\frac{b}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}}=\frac{20}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{62}^{∘}}.
$$

To solve for $b,$ we multiply both sides by $\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}\times \frac{b}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}\times \frac{20}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{62}^{∘}} \\ \cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}}\times \frac{b}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}\times \frac{20}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{62}^{∘}} \\ b & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}\times \frac{20}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{62}^{∘}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}=0.731\,35$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡{62}^{∘}=0.882\,95,$ both rounded to five decimal places to avoid rounding error. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{47}^{∘}\times \frac{20}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{62}^{∘}} \\  & ≈0.731\,35\times \frac{20}{0.882\,95} \\  & ≈\frac{0.731\,35\times 20}{0.882\,95} \\  & ≈\frac{14.627}{0.882\,95} \\  & ≈16.57,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/0df6765fdd30cf0ac74268a4341309a593dd8019c7f66057d36bd4f6c4be5eb2.png)

The Law of Sines states that

$$
\frac{x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡X}=\frac{y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡Y}=\frac{z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡Z}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
m∠X={43}^{∘},\,m∠Y={56}^{∘},\,y=9,
$$

and consequently

$$
\frac{x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}}=\frac{9}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{56}^{∘}}.
$$

To solve for $x,$ we multiply both sides by $\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}\times \frac{x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}\times \frac{9}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{56}^{∘}} \\ \cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}}\times \frac{x}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}\times \frac{9}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{56}^{∘}} \\ x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}\times \frac{9}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{56}^{∘}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}≈0.682$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡{56}^{∘}≈0.829,$ both rounded to four decimal places to avoid rounding error. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘}\times \frac{9}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{56}^{∘}} \\  & ≈0.682\times \frac{9}{0.829} \\  & ≈\frac{0.682\times 9}{0.829} \\  & ≈\frac{6.138}{0.829} \\  & ≈7.4,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem:
In $△LMN,$ we have $m∠N={36}^{∘},$ $MN=9,$ and $LM=6.$ Which of the following statements *could* be true?

I. $∠L$ is acute

II. $m∠L={75.02}^{∘}$ rounded to $2$ decimal places

III. $m∠L={61.85}^{∘}$ rounded to $2$ decimal places
questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/4f5aad8cf0a25781bc08d6ee51b739ecd68f9d2d7a5acc84230ff743739ea533.png)

The law of sines states that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡L}{l}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡N}{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
n=6,\,m∠N={36}^{∘},\,l=9,
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡L}{9} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}}{6} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡L & =9\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘}}{6} \\  & ≈9\cdot \frac{0.587\,79}{6} \\  & ≈0.881\,69,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠L & ≈\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0.881\,69)≈{61.85}^{∘},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠M & ={180}^{∘}-m∠N-m∠L \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{36}^{∘}-{61.85}^{∘} \\  & ≈{82.15}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

However, another solution to $\operatorname{sin}⁡L=0.881\,69$ is given by

$$
m∠L≈{180}^{∘}-{61.85}^{∘}={118.15}^{∘}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠M & ={180}^{∘}-m∠N-m∠L \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{36}^{∘}-{118.15}^{∘} \\  & ≈{25.85}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are two possible triangles, with the following angle measures:

- $m∠L≈{61.85}^{∘},\,m∠M≈{82.15}^{∘},\,m∠N={36}^{∘}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/31d18e2602d9acceccea6a0fe672b4c3f992b12c30c4921b3234e2f22cc454af.png)

- $m∠L≈{118.15}^{∘},\,m∠M≈{25.85}^{∘},\,m∠N={36}^{∘}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/b51c7e3eada7a8e44b0fb9912b95684d77b40e49f8c6bde7859e73f20c6d9f40.png)

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and III only."

In $△ABC,$ we have $m∠A={114}^{∘},$ $AC=5,$ and $BC=9.$ Which of the following statements *could* be true?

I. $∠B$ is acute

II. $m∠C={44.9}^{∘}$ rounded to one decimal place

III. $m∠B={30.5}^{∘}$ rounded to one decimal place
questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/da8f9302098e74dc26c360207d9062d96ac14d17299cf5a2993d70ce45fc69b5.png)

The law of sines states that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}{b}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡A}{a}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
a=9,\,m∠A={114}^{∘},\,b=5,
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}{5} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{114}^{∘}}{9} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡B & =5\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{114}^{∘}}{9} \\  & ≈5\cdot \frac{0.913\,55}{9} \\  & ≈0.507\,53,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places.

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠B & ≈\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0.507\,53)≈{30.5}^{∘},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠C & ≈{180}^{∘}-m∠A-m∠B \\  & ≈{180}^{∘}-{114}^{∘}-{30.5}^{∘} \\  & ≈{35.5}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Another solution to $\operatorname{sin}⁡B≈0.507\,53$ is given by

$$
m∠B≈{180}^{∘}-{30.5}^{∘}≈{149.5}^{∘}.
$$

But we know that a triangle cannot have two obtuse angles. Therefore, there is no triangle that has two angles whose measures are ${114}^{∘}$ and ${149.5}^{∘}.$

So, there is only one possible triangle, with the following angle measures:

$$
m∠A={114}^{∘},\,m∠B≈{30.5}^{∘},\,m∠C≈{35.5}^{∘}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/88208a1751e4af718bac2c58dac144034c6a92d9d5faaf2b9a6861b7f44f32f5.png)

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and III only."

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have the following triangle, where

- Side $a$ is *opposite* angle $A$

- Side $b$ is *opposite* angle $B$

- Side $c$ is *opposite* angle $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/8f3d3bf4824508ef152e8d8d567672d7d61fb36e0ffb533d97be7294e9198956.png)

The **law of sines** states that

$$
\dfrac{a}{\sin{A}} = \dfrac{b}{\sin{B}} = \dfrac{c}{\sin{C}}.
$$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

We can use the law of sines to find an unknown side of the triangle. Let's see an example.

tutorials.name: Using the Law of Sines to Calculate an Acute Angle
tutorials.problem:
Let's again consider the following triangle:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/8f3d3bf4824508ef152e8d8d567672d7d61fb36e0ffb533d97be7294e9198956.png)

The **law of sines** states that

$$
\frac{a}{\sin{A}} = \frac{b}{\sin{B}} = \frac{c}{\sin{C}}.
$$

We can flip the fractions *upside down* to get another formula

$$
\frac{\sin{A}}{a} = \frac{\sin{B}}{b} = \frac{\sin{C}}{c}.
$$

We can use this to find an unknown angle of the triangle.

The **law of sines** states that

$$

We can use the law of sines to find an unknown acute angle of the triangle, but we must *be careful* when using the law of sines to calculate an **obtuse** angle.

The calculator will *always* give an acute angle. If we're trying to find an obtuse angle, we need to subtract our answer from $180^\circ.$

tutorials.name: The Case When Multiple Triangles are Possible
tutorials.problem:
Even if we are given the measure of an angle and two sides of a triangle, it is sometimes possible for two different triangles to satisfy those criteria. 

For example, suppose we are told that in $\triangle ABC,$ we have $m\angle A = 30^\circ,$ $a=4$ and $b=5.$ 

There are two different triangles that satisfy these criteria.

- In one triangle, $\angle B$ is obtuse and $c$ is short:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/7e7abc711536c29313e621d1dab74150647a8463613410d40265ebdf967a9c4d.png)

- In the other triangle, $\angle B$ is acute and $c$ is long:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/77b96c99ddf9bc180934ed28b519f08e2054e91525d881b25ad8318d7b49f777.png)

According to the law of sines, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡A}{a} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}{b} \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘}}{4} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}{5} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡B & =5\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘}}{4} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡B & =5\cdot \frac{0.5}{4} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡B & =0.625\end{aligned}
$$

One solution to the above equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}B & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0.625) \\  & ={38.68}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

This solution corresponds to the second triangle, where $\angle B$ is acute.

However, this is not the only solution. Another solution is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={180}^{∘}-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0.625) \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{38.68}^{∘} \\  & ={141.32}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

This solution corresponds to the first triangle, where $\angle B$ is obtuse.

tutorials.name: Deriving the Law of Sines
tutorials.problem:
Let's now derive the law of sines.

Consider $\triangle ABC$ with sides of lengths $a,b,$ and $c,$ as shown below. Let's assume $\angle A$ is obtuse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/1d30e12e2252b27a651bb02b718cf2214c7ddcf4f0e768c5bd952c11b2e4ecde.png)

Let's add the height perpendicular to $\overline{BC},$ shown below, and let's assume that the length of this height equals $h.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/96817ab2168b9ec37777166a26001ee8bc7e7709f80fdf234ac6d70cdfbb5ddc.png)

Using elementary trigonometry, we have that

$$
\dfrac{h}{b} = \sin C,\qquad \dfrac{h}{c} = \sin B
$$

which gives

$$
h = b\sin C,\qquad h = c\sin B.
$$

Equating the two expressions for $h$ gives

$$
b\sin C = c\sin B.
$$

Dividing this equation by $\sin B\sin C$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}b\operatorname{sin}⁡C & =c\operatorname{sin}⁡B \\ \frac{b\operatorname{sin}⁡C}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B\operatorname{sin}⁡C} & =\frac{c\operatorname{sin}⁡B}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B\operatorname{sin}⁡C} \\ \frac{b\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡C}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡C}} & =\frac{c\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}\operatorname{sin}⁡C} \\ \frac{b}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B} & =\frac{c}{\operatorname{sin}⁡C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also draw a height of length $h'$ perpendicular to the side $AB.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/c5ed139538dd29e2dfaa7435fb45b1a016c333b0169934a15bd74c59a1d68722.png)

According to the diagram, we have

$$
\dfrac{h'}{a} = \sin B,\qquad \dfrac{h'}{b} = \sin (180^\circ - A)
$$

which gives

$$
h' = a\sin B,\qquad h' = b\sin (180^\circ - A).
$$

Equating the two expressions for $h'$ gives

$$
a\sin B = b\sin  (180^\circ - A).
$$

It can be shown that $\sin  (180^\circ - A) = \sin A$ (this essentially states that the sine function is symmetric about $A = 90^\circ,$ which you'll explore in more detail in another lesson). Therefore,

$$
a\sin B = b\sin  A.
$$

Dividing this equation by $\sin A\sin B$ yields

$$
\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}.
$$

Finally, combining this with our previous result, we get

$$
\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}
$$

as required.

Here, we considered the case of an obtuse triangle, where one of the heights we considered lies outside the triangle. The law of sines also applies to acute triangles; the proof is similar.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/1d30e12e2252b27a651bb02b718cf2214c7ddcf4f0e768c5bd952c11b2e4ecde.png)

Let's add the height perpendicular to $\overline{BC},$ shown below, and let's assume that the length of this height equals $h.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/96817ab2168b9ec37777166a26001ee8bc7e7709f80fdf234ac6d70cdfbb5ddc.png)

Using elementary trigonometry, we have that

$$
\dfrac{h}{b} = \sin C,\qquad \dfrac{h}{c} = \sin B
$$

which gives

$$
h = b\sin C,\qquad h = c\sin B.
$$

Equating the two expressions for $h$ gives

$$
b\sin C = c\sin B.
$$

Dividing this equation by $\sin B\sin C$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}b\operatorname{sin}⁡C & =c\operatorname{sin}⁡B \\ \frac{b\operatorname{sin}⁡C}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B\operatorname{sin}⁡C} & =\frac{c\operatorname{sin}⁡B}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B\operatorname{sin}⁡C} \\ \frac{b\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡C}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡C}} & =\frac{c\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡B}\operatorname{sin}⁡C} \\ \frac{b}{\operatorname{sin}⁡B} & =\frac{c}{\operatorname{sin}⁡C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also draw a height of length $h'$ perpendicular to the side $AB.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266767/assets/c5ed139538dd29e2dfaa7435fb45b1a016c333b0169934a15bd74c59a1d68722.png)

According to the diagram, we have

$$
\dfrac{h'}{a} = \sin B,\qquad \dfrac{h'}{b} = \sin (180^\circ - A)
$$

which gives

$$
h' = a\sin B,\qquad h' = b\sin (180^\circ - A).
$$

Equating the two expressions for $h'$ gives

$$
a\sin B = b\sin  (180^\circ - A).
$$

It can be shown that $\sin  (180^\circ - A) = \sin A$ (this essentially states that the sine function is symmetric about $A = 90^\circ,$ which you'll explore in more detail in another lesson). Therefore,

$$
a\sin B = b\sin  A.
$$

Dividing this equation by $\sin A\sin B$ yields

$$
\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}.
$$

Finally, combining this with our previous result, we get

$$
\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}
$$

as required.

Here, we considered the case of an obtuse triangle, where one of the heights we considered lies outside the triangle. The law of sines also applies to acute triangles; the proof is similar.
